source.excerpt: Take thou away from me the noise of thy songs; for I will not hear the melody of thy viols. But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.
trail: The line is Amos 5:24, confirmed word-for-word in the King James Version at Bible Hub ↗.
Later translations render it “justice” rather than “judgment” — compare the side-by-side versions ↗.
Martin Luther King Jr. quoted a paraphrase of this verse near the center of his 1963 “I Have a Dream” speech, as discussed at Conciliar Post ↗.
source.excerptNote: Amos 5:23–24 (KJV). The prophet rejects hollow worship and demands justice in its place.
source.rightsNote: The King James Version was first published in 1611; its text is in the public domain in the United States. This exact English wording — “judgment…a mighty stream” — is the KJV rendering, not a modern in-copyright translation.

author.name: Amos
author.heading: About Amos
author.metaLine: 8th century BC · Hebrew prophet of Israel · Book of Amos, KJV 1611
author.bio: Amos was a herdsman and dresser of sycamore figs from Tekoa in Judah who prophesied in the northern kingdom of Israel around the mid-8th century BC. His book is a searing indictment of empty ritual paired with social injustice, and this verse — demanding that justice and righteousness flow unstoppably — is its most quoted line. The English familiar to most readers here is the King James Version of 1611.

misattribution.heading: The mix-ups
misattribution.intro: The wording asked about is genuine KJV scripture, but it travels with two common confusions.

items.why: King made this verse famous by quoting it — but his celebrated wording, near the center of the 1963 “I Have a Dream” speech ↗, was “justice rolls down like waters,” a paraphrase closer to the RSV/ASV, not the KJV. The line is often credited to King rather than to Amos.
Many quote the KJV verse but substitute “justice” for the KJV’s “judgment.” The translation comparison ↗ shows “justice” belongs to later versions, while the KJV reads “judgment.”

misattribution.truthLine: The exact wording asked about is Amos 5:24 in the King James Version ↗ — genuine, verbatim, and public domain.

context.heading: Why it endures
lead: Amos delivers this line as the climax of a passage rejecting hollow religion: God says he despises Israel’s feasts and songs and wants something else entirely — justice that runs like water. The metaphor of an unstoppable, ever-flowing stream made it a natural rallying cry for reform movements.

In the 20th century it became a touchstone of the American civil-rights movement, above all through Martin Luther King Jr., who returned to it repeatedly. That is why the verse is now heard as much in political speech as in scripture.
